rfm_tuples.R: At December 31, 2024, we were in compliance with our financial covenants under the Credit Agreement. ... rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B test: the October 2024 amendment is a growth-financing amendment, not a covenant relief. Real leverage is ~1.6x vs 3.75x cap — substantial headroom. Disclosure is straight.

rfm_tuples.R: Net service revenues increased by 9.1% to $1,154.6 million for the year ended December 31, 2024 compared to $1,058.7 million in 2023. ... Net service revenue in our personal care segment increased due to a 5.2% increase in revenues per billable hour and a 2.1% increase in billable hours for the year ended December 31, 2024 compared to 2023.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B: derive organic growth net of acquisitions. Filing states 'Acquisitions completed in 2024 accounted for $22.6 million in net service revenues' (mostly 1 month of Gentiva). Compute apples-to-apples organic.
rfm_tuples.M_source: self_text arithmetic on disclosed segment KPIs
rfm_tuples.M_value: Same-store/organic disclosed: personal care same-store rev +7.7% (decelerated from +12.1% prior). Hospice organic +5.9% rev, +1.3% ADC. Home health ORGANIC REVENUE -3.1% (vs -7.1% prior — still negative). Total 9.1% reported growth = $22.6M from acquisitions + organic. Organic ex-acquisition ≈ ($1,154.6 - $22.6 - $1,058.7) / $1,058.7 = 6.9%. Personal-care rev/hour growth (+5.2%) is heavily wage-rate-pass-through driven by state Medicaid rate increases (typical for HCBS) — billable hours grew only 2.1%.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B catches the soft underbelly: home-health organic revenue is still negative, personal-care organic growth is decelerating, and headline 9.1% growth is partially M&A and rate-passthrough rather than volume. Disclosed in tables but minimized in narrative. Not deceptive, but optimistic framing.

rfm_tuples.R: Our consumers are predominantly 'dual eligibles' ... For the year ended December 31, 2024, we derived approximately 61.8% of our net service revenues from state and local governmental agencies, primarily through Medicaid state programs and 22.2% from Medicare. ... In May 2024, CMS finalized a rule ... the '80/20' or 'payment adequacy' requirement, which will require states to ensure that at least 80% of all Medicaid payments a provider receives for homemaker, home health aide, and personal care services ... are spent on total compensation ... for direct care workers ... States are required to ensure compliance with the 80/20 requirement by mid-2030.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B: ADUS personal-care segment operating margin was 20.4% of net service revenues in 2024 (segment op income $174.2M / $856.6M segment revenue). The 80/20 rule directly caps non-direct-care portion at 20% (incl. G&A AND profit). Disclosed risk but not quantified.
rfm_tuples.M_source: self_text + segment financial data from 10-K Item 7
rfm_tuples.M_value: Personal-care segment 2024: revenue $856.6M, segment operating income $174.2M (20.4%). The 80/20 rule would require ≥80% to direct-care worker total compensation. Current direct service personnel cost as % of segment revenue ≈ $617M / $856.6M ≈ 72% (segment-table line 'Direct service personnel') — would need ~$70M shift FROM G&A/profit INTO direct-care comp to comply by mid-2030. Filing says 'it is unclear whether the rule will be implemented as finalized' and 'premature to predict the ultimate impact.' Quantitative impact NOT disclosed. Mid-2030 implementation deadline is genuinely far.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Risk is properly disclosed but not quantified. The 80/20 rule has real teeth for ADUS personal-care economics — current ~72% direct-care comp ratio vs 80% requirement implies meaningful margin pressure unless states allow exclusions or rate increases offset. Filing language ('premature to predict') is honest but glosses the quantification.

Annual impairment test as of Oct 1, 2024 (pre-Gentiva close Dec 2, 2024) — meaning Gentiva goodwill was NOT yet tested. Q1 2025 10-Q shows Texas (Gentiva) generating $49.9M (19.3% of personal-care segment), implying ~$200M annualized run-rate vs. ~$190-220M expected from Gentiva, so on-track. Personal-care gross margin Q1 2025 31.9% vs 31.4% prior — margins held despite mix shift. No impairment indicator triggered yet.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B test: Gentiva run-rate Q1 supports the $353.6M purchase price; no impairment indicator. High goodwill is a structural feature of healthcare roll-ups, not a red flag here. Honest and tracking.

summary: ADUS appears to be an honest disclosure profile. The 10-K and Q1 2025 10-Q are internally consistent, the audit is clean (PwC, unqualified, since 2019, single standard CAM), there is no going-concern language, the Oct 2024 credit-agreement amendment is a capacity-increase for the Gentiva acquisition (not a covenant cure), net leverage is ~1.6x against a 3.75x cap, and CEO insider sales were executed under a pre-existing 10b5-1 plan. Mode-B catches some softness — home-health organic revenue is still negative (-3.1% in FY24), personal-care same-store growth decelerated, and the CMS 80/20 rule represents an unquantified medium-term margin overhang against ADUS's ~72% direct-care comp ratio — but these are disclosed in the segment tables, not concealed. The pre-cutoff -19.1% drawdown looks more like sector de-rating / managed-Medicaid sentiment (CMS rule, Medicaid redeterminations, IDHA concentration) than evidence of operational distress or disclosure dishonesty.
